story|title:100ms copy on write workspac.content_excerpt: Instant, disk-safe workspaces for AI agents on macOS. Clones a prebuilt project tree with APFS clonefile instead of checking out and installing. Replica gives every agent run its own fully installed copy of your project, created in milliseconds with APFS copy-on-write. Each copy is a real git checkout, and automatic cleanup keeps total disk use bounded. Agent workloads are dominated by creating and deleting small files (a checkout, node_modules , build output), and that's where macOS is slowest. A fresh install takes seconds to minutes before the agent does any work. Replica builds a base once: a git clone with its dependencies installed. Each replica new clones that base with one clonefile(2) call. The data blocks stay shared with the base until a file changes, so the new workspace is ready almost at once. Measured on an Apple M1 Max, replica new of a 1,700-file project takes about 100 ms at N = 1 and about 230 ms at N = 10 concurrent workspaces, versus seconds for git clone plus an install. Numbers and methodology . Binaries are published for macOS on Apple Silicon ( arm64 ) and Intel ( x86_64 ). A universal binary covers both. Run replica help for a guided overview, or replica help quickstart to get started. 1. Choose a volume. A dedicated APFS volume with a quota is the safest setup, because clones can never fill your main disk. Any APFS directory works too. Add REPLICA_MAX_BYTES to cap its size. See DISK_SAFETY for the trade-offs. Branches with different lockfiles. If you create a workspace from a branch whose lockfile differs from the base, use --ref : Replica compares the branch's lockfile hash with the base's recorded hash. If they match, the workspace is cloned directly ( cloned directly ). If they differ, Replica clones the base, checks out my-feature-branch , then runs the setup command (an incremental install) so the workspace gets correct dependencies, and reports lockfile drift on branch my-feature-branch; running incremental install . The CLI always tells you which path it took. For agents that open pull requests, the flow is: replica new , work and commit on a branch, push, open the PR with gh pr create , then replica rm . When the remote moves on, replica base refresh updates the base. It does not rebuild from scratch: So an upstream commit that does not touch dependencies costs a fetch and a checkout. A lockfile change costs about as much as the setup command itself. If the fast path fails for any reason, refresh falls back to a full rebu

story|title:agent hive cute grokbot like.content_excerpt: 🐝 One Queen, many bees: an open-source Mac app that turns Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor Agent into a hive. Schedules, event triggers, squads with review loops, a honeycomb view. No API keys. One Queen. Many bees. Your coding agents, working as a hive. A free, open-source Mac app that turns Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, DeepSeek Harness and Cursor Agent into a team you can watch, schedule and steer. Agent Hive is a macOS app that runs several coding-agent CLIs at once and lets them work as a team. Each agent is a bee : Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity ( agy ), DeepSeek Harness ( dsh ), Cursor Agent, or any command you like, working in its own folder. You can talk to each bee, put it on a schedule, chain bees into a relay where one writes and another reviews, or pull them into a group and let Queen hand out the work. It uses the CLIs and logins you already have, including a Claude or ChatGPT subscription. It ships no API keys, stores none, has no account and no server of its own. This downloads the latest release for your Mac (Apple silicon or Intel), puts Agent Hive.app in /Applications and opens it. You can also download the .dmg from the releases page . The app is signed and notarized by Apple. Pull bees into a group and tell Queen what you want. She picks the right bees, dispatches the work, waits for the results and sums them up. She only wakes the bees she needs, and she asks before hatching new ones. A group works without Queen too. @mention a bee and it starts right away. Leave the name out and a small, cheap model picks the bee the message is for, so the others stay asleep; a bee with nothing to add stays quiet. Stickers work both ways. A bee can hand part of the job to another by @mentioning it, for at most three hops. Up to four bees share a folder and pass work down the line. A reviewer can send its findings back to the writer until it approves, for at most three rounds. Bees on the same step run in parallel, each in its own git worktree, and a final bee merges their results. The clip at the top is one such team. A relay team is also a squad with a name. Queen can hand it a whole job with one call and hears back once, when the chain is finished or stuck. You can start it yourself from any group: @Shop-squad add an export button . The group shows the chain and each bee's state as it runs. Each bee has its own chat window with the full conversation. Replies stream in as they are written, edits show as inline di

story|title:agentest offline tests for a.content_excerpt: Agentic evals for AI agents: 165 tests, open source, offline, deterministic, no LLM judge. Reads OpenTelemetry GenAI traces, A2A and MCP. CI-ready. pip install agentest-ai agentest is an open-source tool for agentic evals . It reads the OpenTelemetry traces your agent already recorded and runs 165 tests that judge what the agent actually did, not only what it said: claimed success it did not earn, acted before verifying, followed a hidden instruction, called a tool it should not, or leaked personal data. It runs offline, with no API key, network or LLM judge, so the same traces always give the same verdicts. Install with pip install agentest-ai . The package name is agentest-ai ; the import and the CLI are agentest . A real recorded run of a shopping agent in a mock shop (nothing was bought). Click the image to watch the 56-second video with voiceover . Works with any framework that records OpenTelemetry GenAI traces. Native-log importers: LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, AutoGen, smolagents and n8n. Worked pages: LangGraph , CrewAI , OpenAI Agents SDK . All examples . Agentic evals are tests of an AI agent's actual behaviour — the tools it called, the order it called them, and the state it left behind — rather than only the text it produced. A reply can say the item was added to the cart while the cart is empty; agentic evals read the recorded trace and grade that gap. agentest runs 165 such tests, offline and without an LLM judge. The longer, citable page is What are agentic evals? . Install from PyPI (Python 3.11+, no API key, no model). The package name is agentest-ai ; the import and the agentest command stay agentest : Package page: https://pypi.org/project/agentest-ai/ . To run the latest unreleased code instead, install from GitHub: pip install git+https://github.com/srpadmanabhuni/agentest . From source, three lines (Python 3.11+, no API key, no model). story|title:langsmith tool gateway secur.content_excerpt: Agents are moving beyond the chat window to take on more proactive and ambient work. Instead of waiting for a prompt, they run on a schedule or are triggered by events, and they’re handling longer tasks without someone checking every step. That makes them much more useful, but it also means teams need to control which tools each agent can call and whose identity it acts with, and keep a record of every action it takes. Today, we’re launching LangSmith Tool Gateway in Public Beta, on the LangSmith Agent Platform . Tool Gateway is a managed tool layer that handles credentials, identity, and access for every agent tool call, making it simple to govern the actions your agents take. Tool Gateway makes it easier and faster for engineering teams to grant agents access to new tools in a controlled manner and without hand-rolling auth each time. Security and compliance teams can use LangSmith to trace and audit tool calls as part of agent monitoring. When agents are in production, platform teams need visibility into what each agent did, controls over which tools and models it can use, and usage policies that limit spend and risk. With LangSmith, developers can build, run, and improve agents in a single platform. LLM Gateway governs the model calls agents make. With it, you can set spend limits and model fallbacks, add rate limits, redact personal data and secrets, and provides visibility within the agent trace with rich information on model calls such as latency, fallbacks, failures, guardrails triggered, etc. Tool Gateway lives in LangSmith alongside LLM Gateway, and provides governance across this lifecycle. Tool Gateway simplifies tool lists for agents, implementing policies on usage, managing identity for tool use, and as with LLM Gateway, provides visibility within the agent trace through rich information on tool calls such as servers, users, outcomes, latency, etc. Together, Tool Gateway and LLM Gateway provide comprehensive visibility and governance over agent actions and spend. Agents in production need to serve hundreds or thousands of users, each with their own set of permissions. This means managing and refreshing a large volume of tokens, and carefully managing and recording access for security and audit requirements. Managing identity and visibility at scale is orders of magnitude more difficult than local development. Building this plumbing for every agent individually slows down product delivery and exposes a larger, varied surface area to security r

story|title:llm call is doing more than.content_excerpt: Audiala replaced an LLM router with a decision model and rolled it back 23 minutes later. The replacement could classify intent. The incumbent also resolved cities, conversational references, and tool-control flags. The team had evaluated one responsibility and replaced several. The migration account was one of the clearest examples in Part 1, our survey of decision-model adoption . Other integrations exposed related problems: candidate construction constrained action selection, missing handoff instructions weakened downstream agents, and faster decisions sometimes produced more recovery work. Those reports describe particular implementations, not a universal penalty for specialization. They do suggest a practical starting point: the unit of replacement is the behavior the application depends on. This article follows that idea into the implementation. We will recover a call's contract, construct alternatives, evaluate the complete replacement, and account for keeping it reliable. It appears to select a vendor. But which entity counts as the vendor: the issuing legal entity, a trading name, or the parent company? What happens when two catalog entries share a name? Does a tax identifier override the letterhead? Can the function return an entity absent from the catalog? Does a successful result merely populate a review screen, or does downstream code use it to choose a payment destination? The original prompt may have absorbed several of those responsibilities. It might interpret the invoice, reconcile conflicting evidence, identify an entity, and explain uncertainty in a field the next step reads. A replacement that returns a valid identifier can still lose behavior the application needs. Start with the consumers. Inspect field access, database lookups, tool arguments, intermediate messages, and recovery paths. Read the prompt alongside those dependencies. A field ignored by the immediate caller may still become evidence in a later model call. Conversely, a requested explanation nobody consumes may not belong in the required output. Part 1's LAS case makes this concrete: planners supplied handoff instructions, and reviewers supplied repair guidance. A finite choice could replace one judgment while removing information needed downstream. If that information remains necessary, preserve it or assign its production to another step. story|title:official microsoft agent fra.content_excerpt: Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of the official Microsoft "agent-framework" Python package contain malware - an account compromise is likely The OpenSourceMalware team discovered two malicious releases of Microsoft's agent-framework package on PyPI, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2. Both add a credential stealer that runs automatically whenever Python starts in the affected environment, without anyone importing the package. This isn't a typosquat. The releases came from the legitimate Microsoft-associated PyPI publisher, so trust in the project name, the publisher, lock files or earlier clean releases wouldn't have protected anyone who resolved either version. PyPI has quarantined the publisher, but the threat actor is still believed to have publishing access. It's a reminder that trusted publisher access and Python .pth files both deserve attention. A one-line startup file shipped under an established package name runs before the application's own code and inherits every credential on the developer workstation or CI runner. The stealer searches environment variables, credential files and other processes' environments for secrets. Then it goes further and requests fresh GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps and Azure managed identity tokens, and sends everything to a webhook.site URL hidden in the source as Base64. That combination of passive theft and active token requests makes it especially dangerous in cloud build environments, because even short-lived tokens are useful when they're exfiltrated right away. Treat any installation of 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 as a credential compromise, even if the publisher is restored or a newer version is released. Impact: Theft of developer credentials, CI/CD tokens, cloud identity tokens, application secrets and registry credentials Execution: A .pth file runs the stealer during ordinary Python startup, with no import of the package required Exfiltration: Compressed, Base64-encoded data sent by HTTPS POST to a dedicated webhook.site URL Registry action: PyPI quarantined the Microsoft publisher because unauthorized publishing access is believed to remain active The unpacked 1.26.2 distribution looks plausible at first glance. Its metadata names Microsoft as the author, links to the legitimate Agent Framework project and includes the expected project documentation. The contents tell a different story. Alongside a metadata helper module, it contains two unexpected files: The names suggest harmless runtime diagnostics. Static analysis shows they co

story|title:on device ai new knowledge w.content_excerpt: Viper has an AI chat that runs entirely on your Mac. No cloud. No AI provider account. Your questions never leave the device. It knows Viper. Ask how keys work, how to move to a new phone, what TON Drop does — it answers from Viper's own guides and shows where the answer came from. It can act, too. Ask it to message someone, create an event or save a note, and it prepares a draft. Nothing is sent until you tap Send . What you see. AI Chat in Viper on a Mac, offline. Three everyday questions: what Viper is, how to turn on Face ID login, and what the clock and the single check next to a message mean. Each answer comes with Sources : the in-app guides it was taken from ( Enter via Face ID , Message marks , About Viper ). Tap one to open that guide and check the answer yourself. Why it matters. A messenger's help should not need the internet, an account with an AI company or a support chat. People ask about keys, delivery marks and privacy when something feels wrong — often offline, often in a hurry. Viper answers on the device, from Viper's own guides, and points to the source, so you can trust the answer or check it in one tap. Both point at the same goal: a model on your own device that knows your app and can act in it. We tried both roads for Viper — editing weights and training a small model on Viper. Neither taught a model Viper's facts reliably. What worked was leaving the model alone and building the program around it. We did not retrain the model to teach it Viper. We tried — training facts into the weights made it worse. Instead, Viper builds a harness around an unchanged open model: the knowledge it needs at the moment you ask, the actions it may propose, and checks that run before every build ships. Swap in a better model tomorrow, and everything Viper taught it stays. Viper 1.5.34, now in App Store review, ships gpt-oss-20b on Mac with Viper's knowledge: when you ask about Viper, the app gives the model the About Viper card and the two in-app guides that match your question, and the answer shows those guides as Sources (the screenshot above is 1.5.34). On a small test this worked well: 20 questions about Viper went from 4 right (the model alone) to 19 right (the model with the guides). Twenty questions we wrote ourselves is not proof. So we built a large blind test: At this scale the 1.5.34 approach fell short. On fresh situation-style questions it was right about a third of the time, and invented something in about a third of its answers. Reading

story|title:presentation riiir rewrite i.content_excerpt: A monthly overview of things you need to know as an architect or aspiring architect. Facilitating the Spread of Knowledge and Innovation in Professional Software Development Unlock the full InfoQ experience by logging in! Stay updated with your favorite authors and topics, engage with content, and download exclusive resources. In this episode, Christopher "CRob" Robinson, CTO of OpenSSF, Akrites and Chief Security Architect of the Linux Foundation, explores the state of software supply chain security amid multiple security incidents and explains how tools like Scorecard, the Security Baseline framework, and SLSA help harden software. Jabez Eliezer Manuel discusses the 20-year evolution of Booking.com’s data management and ML platforms. He explains how they scaled MySQL topologies, sunset Hadoop for cloud architecture, and built high-throughput model serving and feature stores operating at 400B predictions per day. He also shares insights on personalization, interleaved experimentation, and their new agentic AI foundation. Nicholas Matsakis shares why AI makes Rust the ideal choice for modern production systems, skipping steep adoption hurdles via compiler guardrails. He discusses Symposium - an open-source, agent-oriented toolchain from the Rust Foundation - and demonstrates how the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) standardizes agent-to-tool extensibility across diverse enterprise developer workflows. Henry Wilson shares actionable tools from the BBC Sounds re-architecture to help senior engineering leaders drive technical strategy. He discusses building buy-in, navigating active resistors, using RFCs and ADRs, and balancing tradeoffs - showing that effective software architecture is fundamentally about communication, relationship-building, and organizational influence. Oli Lane and Julian Wreford share how Gearset replaced guesswork in distributed asynchronous queues with OpenTelemetry tracing. They explain why traditional metrics fall short, how to implement user-centric SLOs based on latency distributions, and share practical debugging tips to help senior developers, software architects, and engineering leaders improve system reliability and team culture. Work through your production AI decisions with senior engineers from other companies. Apply their perspectives to challenges from your own work. Online. Register Now. story|title:running distributed ml and a.content_excerpt: While the hype around Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) promises limitless benefits, the discussion is shifting from theory to real-world practicalities. Focus within platform engineering teams is turning to the usability and operational efficiency of ML/AI, and the viability of running AI workloads at the edge. With this in mind, Cosmonic CTO Bailey Hayes takes a closer look at AI inference, and the ways WebAssembly (Wasm), and platforms like wasmCloud, could improve the effectiveness of distributed AI workloads. AI inference is the process of running live data through a trained AI model to predict an outcome or solve a problem. It is the acid test that reveals how well it puts learned information into practice to make a prediction. Efficient inferencing means AI systems provide fast, accurate outputs. Cloud-only ML and AI strategies have limitations. Moving large volumes of data between clouds and edges is expensive, especially between regions. Latency issues affect AI inference in the cloud, creating lag across devices and cloud environments. Additionally, running AI applications in network-constrained environments impacts application reliability and security, a major problem when delivering real-time services. Wasm is an excellent compilation target for inferencing-style workloads due to its portable, light weight, open architecture, and near-native speed. Its fast startup time and low resource consumption make it ideal for real-time inferencing on edge devices, while secure sandboxing ensures safe operation in diverse environments. Bailey takes us through the current methods for taking advantage of Wasm in AI workloads: wasi-nn , wasi-webgpu , custom interfaces, and providers. Each model is suited to specific use cases—Bailey takes us through the pros and cons. She rounds off the talk with an exciting demo of a celestial and terrestrial mesh running in wasmCloud, exploring how it uses Ollama for image recognition. Check out the recording above, and we’ve dropped the main talking points and talk transcript below. AI inference and Wasm : Wasm is an excellent compilation target for inferencing-style workloads. There are four main approaches, all compatible with wasmCloud: wasi-nn , wasi-webgpu , custom interfaces, and providers. Introduction to wasi-nn : wasi-nn integrates with existing ecosystems, making it ideal where there’s significant investment in existing ML models. story|ver:1.0|title:eve 1 0 agent framew.content_excerpt: Today we're announcing eve 1.0 , the open-source framework for building production-ready agents. Since the public preview in June , we've worked with early adopters to prepare eve for 1.0, shipping 230+ releases and merging thousands of pull requests. With this release, eve is now generally available. We've made eve faster, expanded integrations, and improved observability. Security controls let you decide which actions need approval and what data gets collected. We've also made it easier for coding agents to build with, measuring that experience with a rigorous evaluation suite. With eve handling your harness and infrastructure, you and your agent can focus on building instead. The harness in eve is the loop that calls models, runs tools, and delegates work to subagents. You choose the model, add or replace tools, edit instructions, and decide which actions need approval. The open-source Workflow SDK saves progress as the agent runs, so it can pick up from its last completed step after a crash. Multiplayer sessions and agent-to-agent calls are built in. For managed hosting, deploy your eve agent to Vercel. Vercel Workflows handles durable execution, and Vercel Sandbox runs agent-generated code in isolation. Build software factories that turn requests into tested pull requests, company brains that answer questions from your business data, or customer-facing agents in your product. Thousands of businesses already run eve in production for internal and customer-facing agents. Rillet built a software factory on eve that takes in customer requests, converts them into specs, tests the changes, and opens PRs for human review. Rillet tripled its shipping rate in three months. Clay built monty, a data agent that answers employees’ questions in Slack. Just over two months in, 30–40% of the company used it every week. Multiplayer lets several people work with an agent in one shared session. eve keeps track of who said what and directs approvals and sign-ins to the right person. You can set up memory for each user or the whole team. In the native Slack channel , each thread is one shared session. Approvals appear as buttons that only the right person can answer, and a live task card shows progress and timing. You can follow up in the thread without mentioning the agent again, cancel the current turn, or reset the session from Slack.
